# UK airline data July 2023

Airline activities including route capacity and fleet information.

The CAA collects statistics from all United Kingdom airlines. Monthly aggregate information is supplied on each route served together with quarterly returns of fleet and personnel data and, for the major carriers, annual standardised profit and loss accounts and balance sheets.

From the individual route level data it is possible to build up pictures of the activity of each airline. In addition the traffic and capacity on each route can be assessed. Airline statistics are available as monthly or annual publications or you may commission reports, within certain confidentiality constraints, to suit your particular needs. Historic files include annual and monthly data.

To facilitate improved download times and greater flexibility of use of our data, each table, from June 2001 for airport and punctuality data, and May 2001 for airline data, is available in two formats.

*   PDF files. To view all of the documents on this web site you must have Adobe Acrobat Reader. This is available free of charge from the Adobe web site.
*   Comma Separated Value (CSV), suitable for filtering and sorting, in a spreadsheet application.

Note: Some PDF files contain notes concerning the data within them, the notes are not shown in the respective CSV files; hence the CSV file should always be used in conjunction with the corresponding PDF file.

## How to contact us

If you have feedback on our published reports contact[Aviation.Intelligence@caa.co.uk](mailto:Aviation.Intelligence@caa.co.uk). You will receive an automated reply confirming that we have received your comments.

We review every comment that we receive and, if significant issues are found with our published reporting, reports will be amended and re-published. Unfortunately, we are unable to respond to individual queries.

_As at 25th September 2023 July 2023 data are complete._

_8th February 2024 - March-August 2023 data has been updated to show corrected British Airways Plc / BA Euroflyer Ltd dba British Airways data._

# UK air traffic control failures: the record, the cost and what changed

On 8 September 2026 the NATS flight data system failed for the second time in three years and the airlines cancelled flights for two days. This page puts the incident against the official record: what the reviews of 2014 and 2023 found, what NATS delivers on a normal day, how UK airspace compares with Europe, and why an afternoon's fault at Swanwick becomes a weekend of cancellations at Heathrow.

How to read this

Every figure comes from an official document: NATS's own incident updates and annual reports, the CAA's independent review reports, the NESO review of the Heathrow substation fire, Eurocontrol's Performance Review Unit data and the CAA's airport and punctuality statistics. Press estimates of flights cancelled this week conflict by a factor of two and are quoted only as reported, never charted. NATS's own delay metric counts only delay NATS caused; Eurocontrol's counts all en route delay in UK airspace including weather. The two are shown separately and never combined.

8 September 2026

## What happened, in NATS's own words

NATS posted timed updates through the afternoon and evening of Tuesday 8 September. The fault was in the flight processing system, the same class of system that failed on 28 August 2023. No official count of flights cancelled or passengers affected across the network has been published; British Airways has published its own.

NATS technical issue updates, Tuesday 8 September 2026

1.   13:46"We are investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures."
2.   15:25"We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system."
3.   16:40"Our flight system is starting to recover."
4.   19:30"Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally."
5.   22:10"This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover."
6.   12:55, 9 Sep"We apologise unreservedly" to passengers, airlines and airports, with a fuller investigation to follow.

> "A four-hour air traffic outage yesterday left hundreds of thousands of passengers facing cancellations, diversions and delays. I apologise wholeheartedly to passengers for that disruption. [...] While my understanding from that is that we can rule out a cyber-attack on this occasion, I do not believe this issue was unavoidable. [...] I have therefore asked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review, to establish cause and ensure that our air traffic control systems can get passengers where they need to be. The review will report to me within six months."
> 
> [Heidi Alexander, Secretary of State for Transport, House of Commons, 9 September 2026 ↗](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2026-09-09/debates/6C5383D5-9F16-4D14-AE67-627ADA105C3C/CivilAviation(ConsumerProtectionAndRegulatoryReform)Bill(Lords))

> "When we had the major outage in 2023, it took two years for the CAA to make a similar report. In that report, it made 34 recommendations, of which 32 have been implemented, so a six-month timeframe is a much shorter, sharper window in which to get definitive answers to these questions. NATS is also required to provide a report to the CAA within a week of the incident taking place, to fully explain the implications of what has happened." Later in the debate he corrected the count: "not 32 but all 34 of the recommendations have been implemented."
> 
> [Keir Mather, aviation minister, closing the same debate ↗](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2026-09-09/debates/6C5383D5-9F16-4D14-AE67-627ADA105C3C/CivilAviation(ConsumerProtectionAndRegulatoryReform)Bill(Lords))

> "The technical issue led to delays and the cancellation of hundreds of UK arriving and departing flights on 8 September. [...] We consider that disruption caused by the NATS outage is likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules. This means that although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident."

> [Civil Aviation Authority statement, 9 September 2026 ↗](https://www.caa.co.uk/newsroom/news/caa-statement-on-passenger-compensation-following-nats-disruption-on-8-september/)

Reported, not official: press and wire coverage put UK flight cancellations at "close to 1,000" (PA), "more than 1,000" (Euronews) and "at least 2,000" (other outlets). Neither NATS nor the CAA had published a figure by 10 September. This page does not chart any of them.

The Secretary of State's statement opened the second reading of the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill; the Official Report was retrieved through the Hansard API. No Department for Transport press release on the incident had appeared on gov.uk by 10 September.

The record

## Four NATS technical failures since 2014, and one substation fire

Each card carries only figures the official review or the operator itself published. Where an official count does not exist the card says so.

12 December 2014

### Swanwick: a latent software fault from the 1990s

System Flight server at the London Area Control Centre, Swanwick

Duration 14:44 failure to 20:30 last restriction lifted

*   Both channels of the System Flight Server failed at once for the first time in its history, because of a latent software fault present since the 1990s in a check on the maximum number of controller and supervisor roles.
*   All departures from London airports were stopped at 14:55, and from European airports routing through UK airspace at 15:00. The system was back with controllers at 15:49 without full redundancy; full redundancy returned at 20:10.
*   NATS calculated 14,863 minutes of delay across 353 flights, about 150 cancellations and up to 20 diversions, with 65,000 passengers directly affected. Counting knock on effects NATS's own upper estimate was 1,900 flights and 230,000 passengers.

[CAA and NATS joint independent enquiry, final report, May 2015 ↗](https://www.caa.co.uk/media/r42hircd/nats-system-failure-12-12-14-independent-enquiry-final-report-2-0-1.pdf)

28 August 2023

### The flight plan that shut the system down

System Flight plan processing system (FPRSA-R), Swanwick

Duration Flight plan processing cut from about 800 an hour to about 60 for several hours; disruption ran into the following weekend

*   A single flight plan from Los Angeles to Paris Orly carried two waypoints with the same abbreviation. The software could not resolve it, raised a critical exception, and both the primary and the backup system put themselves into maintenance mode.
*   The CAA estimated over 700,000 passengers affected: about 300,000 by cancellations, about 95,000 by delays of more than three hours and at least 300,000 by shorter delays.
*   The CAA put the cost to airlines at about £65m and the wider cost of the incident at £75m to £100m. None of the passengers were entitled to fixed compensation, because the failure was treated as an extraordinary circumstance outside the airlines' control.
*   NATS's own investigation report put the count at "likely that the number exceeds 1,500" flights cancelled on 28 August, with more the next day; of the 5,500 flights that did operate in UK airspace around 575 were delayed by the incident. About 75 per cent of planned flights operated.
*   The Independent Review Panel made 34 recommendations to NATS, the CAA, airlines, airports and government.

[CAA CAP2993, Independent Review, published 14 November 2024, and CAP2993C, NATS Major Incident Investigation Final Report ↗](https://www.caa.co.uk/CAP2993)

21 March 2025

### Heathrow closed by a fire it did not own

System North Hyde 275kV substation, National Grid, feeding Heathrow through SSEN's network

Duration Closure decided at 01:11; reopened for some repositioning flights that evening; normal operation on 22 March

*   A high voltage bushing on a supergrid transformer failed catastrophically and the transformer oil caught fire. NESO found that a fire risk assessment in July 2024 had said a fire on any of the three transformers "would not be suitably suppressed", and the resulting high priority action was still outstanding in March 2025.
*   Power returned to the North Hyde 66kV substation at 09:49 on 21 March, more than eight hours after Heathrow decided to close. Heathrow reopened for some repositioning and repatriation flights that day and for business as usual on Saturday 22 March.
*   NESO's review is an energy system review. It does not publish a count of flights or passengers affected, and Heathrow's own commissioned Kelly review PDF was no longer at its published address when checked on 10 September 2026, so no official aviation count is shown here.

[NESO, North Hyde Review, interim report, May 2025 ↗](https://www.neso.energy/document/360076/download)

30 July 2025

### A radar fault, fixed in 42 minutes

System Radar related system, Swanwick

Duration Capacity restored within 42 minutes by switching to a backup; flow restrictions while the issue was investigated

*   NATS's annual report describes it as the one material impact on service in the year: "a radar-related technical incident in July 2025 which required us to regulate the flow of air traffic temporarily while the issue was investigated and resolved."
*   NATS's own estimate: 26,134 minutes of delay and approximately 150 cancellations, equivalent to an average of 3.5 minutes of delay for every flight that day.
*   The Transport Secretary met the NATS chief executive the following day. The same report records that "all actions arising from the August 2023 and July 2025 incidents were completed".

[NATS Holdings Annual Report and Accounts 2026, year to 31 March 2026 ↗](https://www.nats.aero/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/NATS11958_AnnualReport-2026_v6.pdf)

8 September 2026

### The flight processing system, again

System Flight processing system, Swanwick

Duration 13:46 first notice to 19:30 "operating normally"; network recovery ran into 9 September

*   NATS identified the fault in its flight processing system at 15:25, reported recovery under way at 16:40 and the system resolved at 19:30, then at 22:10 warned of "a very complex recovery" for the whole network.
*   British Airways cancelled almost 550 flights affecting more than 85,000 of its customers, and more than 190 further flights on 9 September.
*   No network wide count of flights cancelled or passengers affected had been published by NATS, the CAA or the Department for Transport by 10 September. NATS has promised a fuller investigation.

[NATS technical issue updates, 8 to 9 September 2026; British Airways media centre, 9 September 2026 ↗](https://www.nats.aero/news/technical-issue-causing-some-disruption-to-flight-departures/)

The 2018 Gatwick drone closure is left out: the one primary source that carries a reconciled official count, the House of Commons Library briefing on civilian drones, was behind a bot check on every attempt and the press figures conflict.

The 2023 review

## Thirty four recommendations, all implemented

The CAA's Independent Review Panel, chaired by Jeff Halliwell, reported in November 2024. Its recommendations went to NATS, the CAA, airlines, airports and government. The 8 September failure lands against a record in which every recommendation has been signed off as implemented, by NATS in June and by the minister on 9 September.

> What went wrong in 2023
> 
> 
> "In the case of both the primary and the secondary systems, processing of the flight data resulted in critical exception errors being generated which triggered firstly the primary system and then the secondary system to enter maintenance mode."

> On resilience
> 
> 
> Recommendation 20: "NERL should review its strategic approach to resilience, as is common among other safety-critical regulated sectors, recognising the importance to the public of resilience alongside safety and efficiency."

> On counting the damage
> 
> 
> Recommendation 16: "The CAA should explore ways of measuring cancellations and knock-on delays attributable to NERL for use in its incentive framework." The panel "attempted in vain to get objective quantitative information about the extent of the impact" and airlines declined to share passenger lists.

> On who pays
> 
> 
> "None of the over 700,000 passengers estimated to have been impacted by the incident were entitled to such compensation since it was considered to be an 'extraordinary circumstance', though they were entitled to reimbursement of reasonable costs incurred."

July 2025 · Department for Transport, written statement

"NATS has delivered its recommendations with many of these already having been confirmed as completed by the CAA." The CAA expected "most of the recommendations made by the panel will have been validated and completed by the end of 2026."

[Source ↗](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/nats-technical-failure-of-august-2023-caa-progress-report-on-review-recommendations)

June 2026 · NATS Holdings, Annual Report 2026

"All actions arising from the August 2023 and July 2025 incidents were completed. The CAA subsequently noted in the report to the Department for Transport, that NATS response to the 30 July 2025 incident effectively mitigated the risk of a recurrence and confirmed that recommendations from the 2023 independent review have been embedded within regulatory oversight."

[Source ↗](https://www.nats.aero/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/NATS11958_AnnualReport-2026_v6.pdf)

9 September 2026 · Keir Mather, aviation minister, House of Commons

"In that report, it made 34 recommendations, of which 32 have been implemented." Corrected later in the same debate: "I should add that I was slightly remiss in what I said earlier: not 32 but all 34 of the recommendations have been implemented."

[Source ↗](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2026-09-09/debates/6C5383D5-9F16-4D14-AE67-627ADA105C3C/CivilAviation(ConsumerProtectionAndRegulatoryReform)Bill(Lords))

The same annual report records £215.5m of capital spending in the year, "including to accelerate the replacement of the National Airspace System Flight Data Processor". The replacement had not arrived by 8 September 2026.

NATS in normal times

## Very efficient on the average day

The regulator's headline metric for NATS is average delay per flight attributable to its en route operation, in seconds, against a target set in the CAA's NR23 price control. On that measure NATS has beaten the target in each of the last two years. The metric is an average across every flight in the year, so an afternoon that cancels a thousand flights moves it by a few seconds.

## UK airspace is among the least delayed in Europe

Eurocontrol's Performance Review Unit publishes daily en route air traffic flow management delay for every air navigation service provider in Europe. This counts all en route delay in the provider's airspace, whatever the cause, so it is broader than NATS's own attributable figure. ## Heathrow has almost no room to catch up

A three hour restriction at Swanwick becomes two days of cancellations because the airports it feeds run close to full. Heathrow's planning permission caps it at 480,000 air transport movements a year. In 2025 it flew 477,870, leaving 2,130 spare, and scheduled more than the cap before cancellations. Who runs it and who pays

## A regulated monopoly the state half owns

NATS is a public private partnership formed in 2001. Its subsidiary NATS (En Route) plc holds the licence for en route air traffic control over the UK under Part 1 of the Transport Act 2000, with the CAA as its economic regulator.

UK Government, holds the golden share 49%

The Airline Group, a consortium of UK airlines and pension funds 42%

NATS staff, through the employee share trust 5%

LHR Airports Limited (Heathrow)4%

Shareholdings as stated on NATS's company page. The annual report records four shareholders and no ultimate controlling party.

Airlines

Airlines carry the direct cost of rerouting, care and assistance whatever the cause. For 2023 the CAA estimated their cost at about £65m.

Passengers

An air traffic control failure has been treated as an extraordinary circumstance under UK Regulation 261, so passengers get refunds, rerouting and reasonable expenses but not the fixed compensation of £110 to £520 that applies when the airline is at fault.

NATS

NATS is exposed through the CAA's delay and outage incentives on its price control and through enforcement. The CAA's penalties policy allows a fixed penalty of up to 10 per cent of the licence holder's qualifying turnover and a daily penalty of up to 0.1 per cent. In February 2021 the CAA found that NERL "contravened its statutory and Licence duties and obligations in the period January 2019 to March 2020 in relation to the provision of sufficient staffing resilience in the London Approach Service for users of Stansted and Luton airports".

Caveats & data notes

*   No official count of flights cancelled or passengers affected by the 8 September 2026 failure existed on 10 September 2026. Press figures are quoted as reported and not used in any chart or calculation.
*   NATS's average delay per flight is a calendar year regulatory metric counting only delay attributable to NATS's en route operation. Eurocontrol's en route ATFM delay counts all en route delay in the provider's airspace, weather and staffing included. They are different measures of different things and are never combined.
*   NATS flights handled are financial years to 31 March and include oceanic traffic; Eurocontrol's UK count is calendar year continental IFR traffic. They agree within a few per cent, as expected, not exactly.
*   The CAA's on time definition is any degree early through 15 minutes late. The computed 2025 figures reproduce the CAA's own On Time Performance Table to within 0.001 of a percentage point and the build fails if they do not.
*   The 2026 punctuality figures cover January to June 2026, the latest month published, and do not include the September failure. The CAA publishes with a lag of two to three months.
*   The Heathrow cap comparison uses movements flown (Table 04a, total excluding cancelled), which is what a planning condition on movements restricts. Scheduled movements are shown for context only.
*   The December 2018 Gatwick drone closure is omitted because no primary source with a reconciled count could be reached.
*   The Kelly review commissioned by Heathrow was not at its published address when checked; the Heathrow card relies on the NESO review, which does not count flights or passengers.

# UK air traffic control failures: the record, the cost and what changed

On 8 September 2026 the NATS flight data system failed for the second time in three years and the airlines cancelled flights for two days. This page puts the incident against the official record: what the reviews of 2014 and 2023 found, what NATS delivers on a normal day, how UK airspace compares with Europe, and why an afternoon's fault at Swanwick becomes a weekend of cancellations at Heathrow.

Press estimates of flights cancelled this week conflict by a factor of two and are quoted only as reported, never charted. NATS's own delay metric counts only delay NATS caused; Eurocontrol's counts all en route delay in UK airspace including weather. The two are shown separately and never combined.

The record

## Four NATS technical failures since 2014, and one substation fire

Each card carries only figures the official review or the operator itself published. Where an official count does not exist the card says so.

12 December 2014

### Swanwick: a latent software fault from the 1990s

System Flight server at the London Area Control Centre, Swanwick

Duration 14:44 failure to 20:30 last restriction lifted

*   Both channels of the System Flight Server failed at once for the first time in its history, because of a latent software fault present since the 1990s in a check on the maximum number of controller and supervisor roles.
*   All departures from London airports were stopped at 14:55, and from European airports routing through UK airspace at 15:00. The system was back with controllers at 15:49 without full redundancy; full redundancy returned at 20:10.
*   NATS calculated 14,863 minutes of delay across 353 flights, about 150 cancellations and up to 20 diversions, with 65,000 passengers directly affected. Counting knock on effects NATS's own upper estimate was 1,900 flights and 230,000 passengers.

[CAA and NATS joint independent enquiry, final report, May 2015 ↗](https://www.caa.co.uk/media/r42hircd/nats-system-failure-12-12-14-independent-enquiry-final-report-2-0-1.pdf)

28 August 2023

### The flight plan that shut the system down

System Flight plan processing system (FPRSA-R), Swanwick

Duration Flight plan processing cut from about 800 an hour to about 60 for several hours; disruption ran into the following weekend

*   A single flight plan from Los Angeles to Paris Orly carried two waypoints with the same abbreviation. The software could not resolve it, raised a critical exception, and both the primary and the backup system put themselves into maintenance mode.
*   The CAA estimated over 700,000 passengers affected: about 300,000 by cancellations, about 95,000 by delays of more than three hours and at least 300,000 by shorter delays.
*   The CAA put the cost to airlines at about £65m and the wider cost of the incident at £75m to £100m. None of the passengers were entitled to fixed compensation, because the failure was treated as an extraordinary circumstance outside the airlines' control.
*   NATS's own investigation report put the count at "likely that the number exceeds 1,500" flights cancelled on 28 August, with more the next day; of the 5,500 flights that did operate in UK airspace around 575 were delayed by the incident. About 75 per cent of planned flights operated.
*   The Independent Review Panel made 34 recommendations to NATS, the CAA, airlines, airports and government.

[CAA CAP2993, Independent Review, published 14 November 2024, and CAP2993C, NATS Major Incident Investigation Final Report ↗](https://www.caa.co.uk/CAP2993)

21 March 2025

### Heathrow closed by a fire it did not own

System North Hyde 275kV substation, National Grid, feeding Heathrow through SSEN's network

Duration Closure decided at 01:11; reopened for some repositioning flights that evening; normal operation on 22 March

*   A high voltage bushing on a supergrid transformer failed catastrophically and the transformer oil caught fire. NESO found that a fire risk assessment in July 2024 had said a fire on any of the three transformers "would not be suitably suppressed", and the resulting high priority action was still outstanding in March 2025.
*   Power returned to the North Hyde 66kV substation at 09:49 on 21 March, more than eight hours after Heathrow decided to close. Heathrow reopened for some repositioning and repatriation flights that day and for business as usual on Saturday 22 March.
*   NESO's review is an energy system review. It does not publish a count of flights or passengers affected, and Heathrow's own commissioned Kelly review PDF was no longer at its published address when checked on 10 September 2026, so no official aviation count is shown here.

[NESO, North Hyde Review, interim report, May 2025 ↗](https://www.neso.energy/document/360076/download)

30 July 2025

### A radar fault, fixed in 42 minutes

System Radar related system, Swanwick

Duration Capacity restored within 42 minutes by switching to a backup; flow restrictions while the issue was investigated

*   NATS's annual report describes it as the one material impact on service in the year: "a radar-related technical incident in July 2025 which required us to regulate the flow of air traffic temporarily while the issue was investigated and resolved."
*   NATS's own estimate: 26,134 minutes of delay and approximately 150 cancellations, equivalent to an average of 3.5 minutes of delay for every flight that day.
*   The Transport Secretary met the NATS chief executive the following day. The same report records that "all actions arising from the August 2023 and July 2025 incidents were completed".

[NATS Holdings Annual Report and Accounts 2026, year to 31 March 2026 ↗](https://www.nats.aero/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/NATS11958_AnnualReport-2026_v6.pdf)

8 September 2026

### The flight processing system, again

System Flight processing system, Swanwick

Duration 13:46 first notice to 19:30 "operating normally"; network recovery ran into 9 September

*   NATS identified the fault in its flight processing system at 15:25, reported recovery under way at 16:40 and the system resolved at 19:30, then at 22:10 warned of "a very complex recovery" for the whole network.
*   British Airways cancelled almost 550 flights affecting more than 85,000 of its customers, and more than 190 further flights on 9 September.
*   No network wide count of flights cancelled or passengers affected had been published by NATS, the CAA or the Department for Transport by 10 September. NATS has promised a fuller investigation.

[NATS technical issue updates, 8 to 9 September 2026; British Airways media centre, 9 September 2026 ↗](https://www.nats.aero/news/technical-issue-causing-some-disruption-to-flight-departures/)

The 2023 review

## Thirty four recommendations, all implemented

The CAA's Independent Review Panel, chaired by Jeff Halliwell, reported in November 2024. Its recommendations went to NATS, the CAA, airlines, airports and government. The 8 September failure lands against a record in which every recommendation has been signed off as implemented, by NATS in June and by the minister on 9 September.

> What went wrong in 2023
> 
> 
> "In the case of both the primary and the secondary systems, processing of the flight data resulted in critical exception errors being generated which triggered firstly the primary system and then the secondary system to enter maintenance mode."

> On resilience
> 
> 
> Recommendation 20: "NERL should review its strategic approach to resilience, as is common among other safety-critical regulated sectors, recognising the importance to the public of resilience alongside safety and efficiency."

> On counting the damage
> 
> 
> Recommendation 16: "The CAA should explore ways of measuring cancellations and knock-on delays attributable to NERL for use in its incentive framework." The panel "attempted in vain to get objective quantitative information about the extent of the impact" and airlines declined to share passenger lists.

> On who pays
> 
> 
> "None of the over 700,000 passengers estimated to have been impacted by the incident were entitled to such compensation since it was considered to be an 'extraordinary circumstance', though they were entitled to reimbursement of reasonable costs incurred."

"NATS has delivered its recommendations with many of these already having been confirmed as completed by the CAA." The CAA expected "most of the recommendations made by the panel will have been validated and completed by the end of 2026."

June 2026 · NATS Holdings, Annual Report 2026

"All actions arising from the August 2023 and July 2025 incidents were completed. The CAA subsequently noted in the report to the Department for Transport, that NATS response to the 30 July 2025 incident effectively mitigated the risk of a recurrence and confirmed that recommendations from the 2023 independent review have been embedded within regulatory oversight."

[Source ↗](https://www.nats.aero/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/NATS11958_AnnualReport-2026_v6.pdf)

9 September 2026 · Keir Mather, aviation minister, House of Commons

"In that report, it made 34 recommendations, of which 32 have been implemented." Corrected later in the same debate: "I should add that I was slightly remiss in what I said earlier: not 32 but all 34 of the recommendations have been implemented."

[Source ↗](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2026-09-09/debates/6C5383D5-9F16-4D14-AE67-627ADA105C3C/CivilAviation(ConsumerProtectionAndRegulatoryReform)Bill(Lords))

The same annual report records £215.5m of capital spending in the year, "including to accelerate the replacement of the National Airspace System Flight Data Processor". The replacement had not arrived by 8 September 2026.

NATS in normal times

## Very efficient on the average day

The regulator's headline metric for NATS is average delay per flight attributable to its en route operation, in seconds, against a target set in the CAA's NR23 price control. On that measure NATS has beaten the target in each of the last two years. The metric is an average across every flight in the year, so an afternoon that cancels a thousand flights moves it by a few seconds.

This counts all en route delay in the provider's airspace, whatever the cause, so it is broader than NATS's own attributable figure. A three hour restriction at Swanwick becomes two days of cancellations because the airports it feeds run close to full. Who runs it and who pays

## A regulated monopoly the state half owns

NATS is a public private partnership formed in 2001. Its subsidiary NATS (En Route) plc holds the licence for en route air traffic control over the UK under Part 1 of the Transport Act 2000, with the CAA as its economic regulator.

UK Government, holds the golden share 49%

The Airline Group, a consortium of UK airlines and pension funds 42%

NATS staff, through the employee share trust 5%

LHR Airports Limited (Heathrow)4%

Shareholdings as stated on NATS's company page. The annual report records four shareholders and no ultimate controlling party.

Airlines

Airlines carry the direct cost of rerouting, care and assistance whatever the cause. For 2023 the CAA estimated their cost at about £65m.

Passengers

An air traffic control failure has been treated as an extraordinary circumstance under UK Regulation 261, so passengers get refunds, rerouting and reasonable expenses but not the fixed compensation of £110 to £520 that applies when the airline is at fault.

NATS

NATS is exposed through the CAA's delay and outage incentives on its price control and through enforcement. The CAA's penalties policy allows a fixed penalty of up to 10 per cent of the licence holder's qualifying turnover and a daily penalty of up to 0.1 per cent. In February 2021 the CAA found that NERL "contravened its statutory and Licence duties and obligations in the period January 2019 to March 2020 in relation to the provision of sufficient staffing resilience in the London Approach Service for users of Stansted and Luton airports".

What is not published

## The numbers that should exist by now

How many flights were cancelled on 8 and 9 September 2026?

Not published

The CAA said "hundreds" of flights; the Secretary of State said "hundreds of thousands of passengers". Press figures range from about 1,000 to at least 2,000 flights. NATS's report to the CAA is due within a week. The 2023 review had recommended the CAA "explore ways of measuring cancellations and knock-on delays".

How many flights were cancelled on 28 August 2023?

Only NATS's own estimate

The CAA's review gives passengers (over 700,000) and cost (£75m to £100m) but shows daily cancellations only as a chart. The count in the record is NATS's own: "likely that the number exceeds 1,500". The widely quoted 1,585 does not appear in either report.

How many passengers did the Heathrow closure affect?

No official count found

NESO's review is an energy review. Heathrow's Kelly review PDF was not at its published address on 10 September 2026.

What did the 8 September failure cost?

Not yet known

For 2023 the CAA produced an estimate in its final report, fourteen months after the event.

Questions this raises

## What the investigation should answer

1.   1.
Was the 8 September fault in the same flight data processing system that failed in 2023, and if so which of the 34 recommendations was supposed to prevent a recurrence?

2.   2.
When will the replacement flight data processor that NATS was "accelerating" in its 2026 annual report enter service, and what runs in the meantime?

3.   3.
Why is there still no official count of flights cancelled and passengers affected, two years after the review asked the CAA to find a way to measure exactly that?

4.   4.
Should a failure inside a regulated monopoly still count as an extraordinary circumstance that removes passengers' right to compensation?

5.   5.
Does the CAA's outage metric, which only removes NATS's delay bonus above 250 points, put a price on a failure that costs airlines tens of millions?

6.   6.
If Heathrow schedules above its 480,000 movement cap and flies within 2,130 of it, what is the plan for recovering a lost afternoon at the hub?

Caveats & data notes

*   No official count of flights cancelled or passengers affected by the 8 September 2026 failure existed on 10 September 2026. Press figures are quoted as reported and not used in any chart or calculation.
*   NATS's average delay per flight is a calendar year regulatory metric counting only delay attributable to NATS's en route operation. Eurocontrol's en route ATFM delay counts all en route delay in the provider's airspace, weather and staffing included. They are different measures of different things and are never combined.
*   NATS flights handled are financial years to 31 March and include oceanic traffic; Eurocontrol's UK count is calendar year continental IFR traffic. They agree within a few per cent, as expected, not exactly.
*   The CAA's on time definition is any degree early through 15 minutes late. The computed 2025 figures reproduce the CAA's own On Time Performance Table to within 0.001 of a percentage point and the build fails if they do not.

Cutting-edge technology introduced as part of British Airways’ £7bn transformation investment programme has seen the airline boost its operational performance to record levels.

The airline’s Chairman and CEO, Sean Doyle, told the Future Travel Experience World Innovation Summit in Pittsburgh that AI, forecasting, optimisation and machine learning have transformed the airline’s operational performance and become an integral part of getting customers to where they need to be with minimal delay to their travel plans.

Every part of British Airways now uses this latest technology, which has significantly increased the number of flights departing on time or ahead of their scheduled take-off times.

The airline has invested £100m in improving operational resilience and the first quarter of 2025 saw 86 per cent of its flights on time from its London Heathrow base, the highest D-15 punctuality performance on record. This is compared to 46% in 2008.

Throughout the quarter, British Airways flights achieved 90+ per cent on-time departures on 38 of the 89 operational days.

And last month (April), two thirds of all of the airline’s flights departing from Heathrow left ahead of their departure time. This is more than double the number that achieved this for the same period in 2023 and almost 20 per cent more than those that did in 2024.

**Sean Doyle, British Airways Chairman and Chief Executive, said:**

“Improving operational performance is a key part of our investment programme because we know the impact delays and disruption can have on our customers.

“Whilst disruption to our flights is often outside of our control, our focus has been on improving the factors we can directly influence and putting in place the best possible solutions for our customers when it does happen. That’s why we’ve invested £100m in our own operational resilience, putting funding into technology and tools, and devising a better way of working on the ground at Heathrow as well as creating an additional 600 operational roles into the airport.

“The tech colleagues have at their fingertips has been a real gamechanger for performance, giving them the confidence to make informed decisions for our customers based on a rapid assessment of vast amounts of data. It’s exciting that our industry is able to harness this capability, which will develop even further in the months years to come.”

In 2023, British Airways announced a major £7bn investment programme designed to deliver a world-class customer experience and better on-time performance.

A fundamental part of the strategy has been a £100m investment that has seen the development of a range of digital tools and apps designed to boost operational performance. More than 100 data scientists are now employed by the airline, working on projects across the business. In total, around 830 change projects have been rolled out.

The foundation of this work has been improving the performance and resilience of the airline’s systems, including the migration of data centres to the Cloud to bring increased digital stability. This work is now 90 per cent complete.

Across the operation, technical experts have developed an application that means the airline can now allocate aircraft landing at Heathrow to stands based on a live analysis of the onward travel plans of customers on any given flight, cutting missed connections and disruption to onward journeys. This has saved 160,000 minutes of delays.

A real-time weather program that proactively reroutes aircraft to avoid areas of poor weather has also been deployed. It is capable of communicating directly with Air Traffic Control flow management centres across Europe to find and generate more efficient routings and has prevented a total of 243,000 minutes of delays.

The airline is also using a new tool that uses predictive technology to bring together and assess vast amounts of live real-time operational data to highlight routes that could face delays, allowing teams to put in place additional measures to reduce that risk.

Tech-based programmes to help operational colleagues make the best possible decisions during periods of disruption have also been shown to have had a significantly positive impact.

For example, our Runway support tool that calculates the most appropriate schedule intervention when disruption occurs.It uses data from the planned schedule, passengers and crew to determine the most appropriate response to disruption such as cancellations, arrival delays or aircraft changes. It has been used to model 163 disruption event scenarios across 2024 and 2025 to minimise the impact of air traffic control rates and bad weather for customers.

Over the coming months, additional tools and programmes are also being deployed to further improve operational performance. These include new apps for pilots, cabin crew teams and aircraft dispatch teams to help speed-up aircraft departures.

# UK airports see record passenger traffic as aviation heads for its busiest year ever

 Passenger numbers hit 141m in the first half of 2025, signalling UK aviation’s strongest recovery yet and putting the sector on course for a record year. 

[![Image 29: A smiling woman with shoulder-length brown hair and hoop earrings poses for a professional headshot against a teal background.](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Chloe-Greenbank.jpg) Chloe Greenbank](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/writer/chloe-greenbank/?modal=yes)

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has reported a record 81 million passengers passing through the country’s airports between April and June 2025. This is the highest quarterly figure on record for passenger traffic.

Passenger traffic during the first six months of the year totalled 141 million, putting the industry on course for a record-breaking summer and signalling a full return to – and in many cases beyond – pre-pandemic (2019) demand levels.

Operational performance also showed marked improvement, with airline punctuality reaching its strongest level in recent years. According to the CAA 75% of flights are currently departing on time, an 8 % point increase when compared with 2024. [April was a](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/flight-disruption-rights-caa-warning/)**[standout month with 82 % of services operating to schedule](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/flight-disruption-rights-caa-warning/).**

## UK aviation sector is experiencing strong demand

Selina Chada, group director for consumers and markets at the CAA, said the “numbers were a great achievement” with the growth in the UK’s aviation sector reflecting both strong demand and sector-wide efforts to improve reliability.

“Reliable, on-time flights remain a priority, and it’s encouraging that delays are falling year-on-year,“ she said.

London Heathrow has also solidified its position as Europe’s most punctual major airport hub, with more flights departing on time than any other comparable airport. [**The airport is already the UK’s busiest hub, operating close to its capacity**.](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-expansion-10bn-plan-capacity-investment/)

Growth in passenger traffic in the UK further supports the airport’s case for increasing capacity **[with a third runway](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-expansion-third-runway-plans-dft/)**[**.**](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/key-heathrow-numbers-as-government-backs-third-runway/)Not doing so could mean the UK loses out to rival hubs, including Amsterdam, Paris and Frankfurt.

![Image 31: London Heathrow Airport with British Airways aircraft](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/heathrow_17581504373208.jpg)

Photo: Heathrow Airport

Airlines UK chief executive, Tim Alderslade, said the latest figures underpin aviation’s role as a key growth driver for the country’s economy.

“These trends demonstrate the strength of aviation as a growth engine for the UK, boosting the regions and supporting our companies, all whilst delivering improved service standards.”

## Regional airports show their resilience

While the UK’s primary gateway, London Heathrow, welcomed an unprecedented 39.9 million passengers in the first half of 2025, the CAA’s report also highlighted regional resilience, with northern airports seeing impressive gains. Collectively, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle and Leeds Bradford welcomed three-quarters of a million additional passengers compared with the same period last year.

“We are delighted the data shows that UK airports are busier than ever, and punctuality has significantly improved, as the industry surpasses levels last seen before the pandemic,” noted Karen Dee, chief executive of trade body, AirportsUK.

“Air travel sits at the heart of the economy, connecting friends and family, making sure that global tourism is possible, linking UK businesses with new and existing markets and transporting goods worth billions all over the world.”

In terms of passenger traffic, short-haul routes to destinations including Dublin, Amsterdam, Palma de Mallorca and Alicante were all credited with helping to boost growth.

![Image 32: British Airways Airbus A321](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/HawkeyeUK-2048px-Airbus_A321-251NX_%E2%80%98G-NEOR_British_Airways-1024x683.jpg)

British Airways Airbus A321. Photo: HawkeyeUK Wikimedia Commons

The UK’s flag-carrying airline, [**British Airways**,](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?s=british+airways+) has itself noted growth between January and June with its half-year earnings increasing despite a £40 million hit from the **[closure of Heathrow in May following a fire at a nearby substation](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-fire-caused-by-years-old-fault-at-power-substation/)**.

The airline reported a 48% increase in underlying operating profits to £84 million for the first six months to 30 June, up from £555 million in the previous year.

## Freight expectations for the UK’s cargo sector

Cargo also demonstrated its resilience with a robust performance in the first six months of the year. Volumes grew 6% year-on-year, with nearly 700,000 tonnes shipped through UK airports in Q2.

Cargo links with Asia, particularly Mumbai and Delhi, saw strong growth with year-on-year increases of 61% and 41% respectively. Dubai, New York, Doha and Leipzig were all highlighted as popular freight destinations.

![Image 33](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/iStock-1047540990-scaled-1-1024x683.jpg)
Alderslade added that the sector will “continue to prioritise passengers and freight customers and looks forward to working with Government to build on this momentum, so we can secure the future of aviation, the jobs it delivers and the world-class connectivity it provides.”

## What does this growth mean for UK airports in the longer term?

The figures confirm UK aviation’s continued recovery trajectory and are a key indicator of recovery and expansion. This, in turn, will restore confidence among investors, airports and government stakeholders. Passenger growth also boosts regional airports, spreading economic benefits beyond the main city hubs.

The record passenger growth also strengthens the commercial case for airport ownership, with stakes in multiple UK air transport hubs either up for sale or recently sold.

In July, Spanish construction company Ferrovial confirmed it had completed the sale of its remaining 5.25% stake in London Heathrow to **[private equity group Ardian and Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/saudis-stake-their-claim-in-heathrow-alongside-ardian/)**.

The announcement followed Australia’s largest infrastructure investor – Macquarie Asset Management – confirming in June that it was **[acquiring stakes in three UK airports from Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/five-european-airports-up-for-multi-billion-pound-sale/)**. This includes a 25% stake in London City, a 55% share in Bristol Airport and a 26.5% stake in Birmingham.

Meanwhile, in March US private equity firm **[Blackstone struck a £325 million deal to acquire a 22% stake in AGS Airports,](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/avialliance-completes-ags-airports-acquisition-and-appoints-ceo/)**which owns and operates Aberdeen, Glasgow and Southampton.

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has reported a record 81 million passengers passing through the country’s airports between April and June 2025. This is the highest quarterly figure on record for passenger traffic.

Passenger traffic during the first six months of the year totalled 141 million, putting the industry on course for a record-breaking summer and signalling a full return to – and in many cases beyond – pre-pandemic (2019) demand levels.

Operational performance also showed marked improvement, with airline punctuality reaching its strongest level in recent years. According to the CAA 75% of flights are currently departing on time, an 8 % point increase when compared with 2024. [April was a](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/flight-disruption-rights-caa-warning/)**[standout month with 82 % of services operating to schedule](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/flight-disruption-rights-caa-warning/).**

## UK aviation sector is experiencing strong demand

Selina Chada, group director for consumers and markets at the CAA, said the “numbers were a great achievement” with the growth in the UK’s aviation sector reflecting both strong demand and sector-wide efforts to improve reliability.

“Reliable, on-time flights remain a priority, and it’s encouraging that delays are falling year-on-year,“ she said.

London Heathrow has also solidified its position as Europe’s most punctual major airport hub, with more flights departing on time than any other comparable airport. [**The airport is already the UK’s busiest hub, operating close to its capacity**.](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-expansion-10bn-plan-capacity-investment/)

Growth in passenger traffic in the UK further supports the airport’s case for increasing capacity **[with a third runway](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-expansion-third-runway-plans-dft/)**[**.**](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/key-heathrow-numbers-as-government-backs-third-runway/)Not doing so could mean the UK loses out to rival hubs, including Amsterdam, Paris and Frankfurt.

![Image 31: London Heathrow Airport with British Airways aircraft](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/heathrow_17581504373208.jpg)

Photo: Heathrow Airport

Airlines UK chief executive, Tim Alderslade, said the latest figures underpin aviation’s role as a key growth driver for the country’s economy.

“These trends demonstrate the strength of aviation as a growth engine for the UK, boosting the regions and supporting our companies, all whilst delivering improved service standards.”

## Regional airports show their resilience

While the UK’s primary gateway, London Heathrow, welcomed an unprecedented 39.9 million passengers in the first half of 2025, the CAA’s report also highlighted regional resilience, with northern airports seeing impressive gains. Collectively, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle and Leeds Bradford welcomed three-quarters of a million additional passengers compared with the same period last year.

“We are delighted the data shows that UK airports are busier than ever, and punctuality has significantly improved, as the industry surpasses levels last seen before the pandemic,” noted Karen Dee, chief executive of trade body, AirportsUK.

“Air travel sits at the heart of the economy, connecting friends and family, making sure that global tourism is possible, linking UK businesses with new and existing markets and transporting goods worth billions all over the world.”

In terms of passenger traffic, short-haul routes to destinations including Dublin, Amsterdam, Palma de Mallorca and Alicante were all credited with helping to boost growth.

![Image 32: British Airways Airbus A321](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/HawkeyeUK-2048px-Airbus_A321-251NX_%E2%80%98G-NEOR_British_Airways-1024x683.jpg)

British Airways Airbus A321. Photo: HawkeyeUK Wikimedia Commons

The UK’s flag-carrying airline, [**British Airways**,](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?s=british+airways+) has itself noted growth between January and June with its half-year earnings increasing despite a £40 million hit from the **[closure of Heathrow in May following a fire at a nearby substation](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/heathrow-fire-caused-by-years-old-fault-at-power-substation/)**.

The airline reported a 48% increase in underlying operating profits to £84 million for the first six months to 30 June, up from £555 million in the previous year.

## Freight expectations for the UK’s cargo sector

Cargo also demonstrated its resilience with a robust performance in the first six months of the year. Volumes grew 6% year-on-year, with nearly 700,000 tonnes shipped through UK airports in Q2.

Cargo links with Asia, particularly Mumbai and Delhi, saw strong growth with year-on-year increases of 61% and 41% respectively. Dubai, New York, Doha and Leipzig were all highlighted as popular freight destinations.

![Image 33](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/iStock-1047540990-scaled-1-1024x683.jpg)
Alderslade added that the sector will “continue to prioritise passengers and freight customers and looks forward to working with Government to build on this momentum, so we can secure the future of aviation, the jobs it delivers and the world-class connectivity it provides.”

## What does this growth mean for UK airports in the longer term?

The figures confirm UK aviation’s continued recovery trajectory and are a key indicator of recovery and expansion. This, in turn, will restore confidence among investors, airports and government stakeholders. Passenger growth also boosts regional airports, spreading economic benefits beyond the main city hubs.

The record passenger growth also strengthens the commercial case for airport ownership, with stakes in multiple UK air transport hubs either up for sale or recently sold.

In July, Spanish construction company Ferrovial confirmed it had completed the sale of its remaining 5.25% stake in London Heathrow to **[private equity group Ardian and Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/saudis-stake-their-claim-in-heathrow-alongside-ardian/)**.

The announcement followed Australia’s largest infrastructure investor – Macquarie Asset Management – confirming in June that it was **[acquiring stakes in three UK airports from Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/five-european-airports-up-for-multi-billion-pound-sale/)**. This includes a 25% stake in London City, a 55% share in Bristol Airport and a 26.5% stake in Birmingham.

Meanwhile, in March US private equity firm **[Blackstone struck a £325 million deal to acquire a 22% stake in AGS Airports,](https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/avialliance-completes-ags-airports-acquisition-and-appoints-ceo/)**which owns and operates Aberdeen, Glasgow and Southampton.
