## Marketing to the Federal Government

The VA Federal Supply Schedule (FSS) Program is the premier Government program in place to acquire state-of-the-art healthcare-related products and services. Being a Schedule contractor is not a guarantee of sales, and with nearly 2,000 contractors, and more being added every day, competition under the Program is fierce. That said, the VA FSS Service wants you to be a successful industry partner. To do this, you must develop a robust marketing plan that includes clearly defined steps to promote and maintain a relationship with potential government customers while ensuring continued[contracting compliance](https://department.va.gov/procurement-acquisition-and-logistics/national-acquisition-center/federal-supply-schedule-service/?target=Contractor+Responsibilities)with your firm’s awarded pricing, terms, and conditions. Good marketing efforts will help you identify government customers and get their attention so they are motivated to purchase from you.

This page offers resources and strategies for maximizing business opportunities under the VA Schedules Program.

### Marketing a Schedules Contract

**Your Potential Customer Base**: The success of your Schedules contract will require active promotion of your business to potential customers.

Your customer base includes organizations eligible to use GSA Sources of Supply and Services, such as executive and other federal agencies. Through Cooperative Purchasing and Disaster Recovery Purchasing, state and local governments, and even government contractors, can use Schedules.

*   The[VA Facilities site](https://www.va.gov/find-locations)is a storehouse of facility and key staff information within 1728 VA facilities, maintained on a regular basis by editors and administrators nationwide throughout the VA network. Designed for ease-of-use, this site categorizes information for browsing by state and administration, as well as by viewing through an interactive map of the United States.
*   [VA _Advantage!_](https://vaadvantage.gsa.gov/), a partnership between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the General Services Administration, is a commitment towards improving the acquisition process for VA customers. VA _Advantage!_ has been primarily designed to provide the VA user with robust tools for performing market research, as well as a streamlined ordering process for procuring pharmaceutical and medical supplies. _This site requires registration/Login._
*   A huge opportunity for business exists on military installations. The trick is being able to locate the right Program Office. A good place to start is with Armed Forces Network’s list of military installations worldwide, and then narrow your search by region, state, and activity.
*   [FedBizOpps](https://sam.gov/opportunities)(replaced by SAM.gov) is the single source to find federal procurement opportunities that exceed $25,000. Vendors can set up daily email notifications and search procurements by solicitation number, date, procurement classification code, and agency for both active and archived solicitations. With over 51 agencies posting to its website regularly, FBO is a key resource for finding opportunities. Users are not required to register, nor do they require a username and password, to begin using FedBizOpps.
*   Government buyers can post a Request for Quote via[eBuy](http://www.ebuy.gsa.gov/)and Schedules contractors can submit quotes to any RFQ corresponding to the Schedule and Special Item Numbers (SINs) listed in their contract. eBuy is an excellent tool for finding new business and is only available to contractors on Schedule. Users must register to use this site.
*   The[Federal Acquisition Jump Station](https://prod.nais.nasa.gov/pub/fedproc/home.html)provides websites of federal procurement information broken down by agency. You will be able to obtain, among other things, announcements of upcoming and current acquisitions, solicitations, and federal acquisition regulations.
*   SAM.gov is the authoritative source for federal contract Award Data [SAM.gov Contracting](https://sam.gov/contracting)
*   Additionally, you can research[Defense Logistics Agency](http://www.dla.mil/DoingBusinessWithDLA.aspx)and[Department of Navy](https://www.neco.navy.mil/)procurements online.

### Sales Strategies

In addition to the myriad of resources available on the web, these are a few smart strategies that will help maximize your business opportunities. We offer free training materials that can assist with expanding your employees’ knowledgebase about the VA FSS program and your firm’s contract. Additional free training is offered by GSA.

*   **Educate your workforce.** A well trained workforce can make or break a potential sale and ensure repeat business. All employees should at least: 
    *   Know your firm has a VA FSS contract and it’s number;
    *   Be able to identify eligible government customers;
    *   Provide accurate information about your firm’s contract; and
    *   Assist the customer in completing all aspects of the sale.

*   **Find government customers through market research.** Market research is essential to any successful marketing plan. It allows you to find out who is buying and what, when, and where they are buying. By identifying these key elements about your target customer group, you are taking a major step forward in achieving your marketing and purchasing goals. 
    *   Explore[USA.gov](https://www.usa.gov/). This site offers online chat, blogs, news, features, and direct links to government agencies.

*   **Maximize your internet presence.** The internet is rife with opportunities for free or low-cost marketing. By simply providing your web address on your[Authorized FSS Price List](https://department.va.gov/procurement-acquisition-and-logistics/national-acquisition-center/federal-supply-schedule-service/?target=Price+List+Requirements),you have strengthened your marketing foothold. Additionally, social media applications provide a unique way of interacting with your customers. Remember, the government is online too.
*   **Government advertising opportunities.** There are a myriad of publications related to the government acquisition process. These publications afford you an excellent opportunity to reach your target customers through traditional media. Find the appropriate publications for your industry and consider advertising your VA FSS contract in them. Be sure to include a link to your website!

### Purchasing Programs

Additional purchasing programs your company should know about:

*   **Small Business Goals:** If your company is a small, veteran-owned, service-disable veteran-owned, disadvantaged, women-owned, HUBZone business, know that all federal agencies set Small Business Goals, which aim to put a percentage of procurement dollars toward these business categories. Learn more about how to participate through the VA’s[Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization](https://www.va.gov/osdbu/index.asp).
*   **Contractor Team Arrangements (CTAs):** If the scope of your contract cannot meet all of a customer’s requirements, you may work with another contractor. In a CTA, two or more Schedules contractors work together to meet the needs of a customer.
*   **Blanket Purchase Agreements (BPAs):** Setting up a BPA is a way to obtain regular business from a customer with repetitive needs for the product(s) or service(s) you offer. Because a BPA brings in continuous sales, it is appropriate to offer additional price discounts to your customer as part of the agreement.
*   **Small Business Subcontracting Opportunities.** For some small businesses, subcontracting to a Prime Vendor is a great way to “get a foot in the door” of government contracting. In this arrangement, you can provide goods or services that support a larger initiative that you couldn’t handle on your own. And it’s a great way to gain valuable experience! 
    *   [SUB-Net](https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-guide/prime-subcontracting/subcontracting-opportunities): SUBNet Subcontracting Opportunities

_What Qualifies as a Schedules Sale?_ The following shall be reported as FSS sales and the IFF collected and remitted:

*   Orders placed under a Department of Defense Distribution and Pricing Agreement (DAPA) for the following schedules: 65 I B, 621 I, 621 II, and 66 III.

The following are sales that shall not be reported as FSS sales; therefore, an IFF subject to FSS contract terms and conditions shall not be collected and remitted:

### **Trade Agreement Act (TAA)**

_Applicable Regulation:_ 52.225-5 Trade Agreements.

_Requirement:_ The Trade Agreements Act is applicable to all Schedules. In exercising its authority under FAR Part 25, Foreign Acquisition, purchases by Ordering Activities are restricted to either U.S.-made or designated country end products. A U.S.-made product can be either 1) an article that is mined, produced, or manufactured in the United States, or 2) an article that is substantially transformed in the United States into a new and different article of commerce with a name, character, or use distinct from that of the article or articles from which it was transformed. It is the offeror’s responsibility to verify that all offered products are U.S. made or designated country end products as defined in clause FAR 52.225-5. When an item consists of components from various countries and the components are assembled in a designated country, the test to determine country of origin is substantial transformation ([FAR 25.001(c)(2)](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/part-25#FAR_25_001)). For services, origin is determined by the country in which the firm providing the service is established, not the location at which the services are performed.

 Customer Experience

**OUR PROMISE**

For millions of people living with a disability, travel can be difficult – and flying can sometimes feel out of reach. More than one million customers who require additional assistance fly with British Airways each year, and we believe our unique British Airways service should be accessible to everyone.

We’re continually improving our service and our ambition is to become the airline of choice for customers with visible and non-visible disabilities. We are committed to doing everything we can to support customers that require additional assistance and provide a seamless travel experience.

**CONTACTING BRITISH AIRWAYS ’ ACCESSIBILITY TEAM**

*   Our accessibility team can be contacted in the UK via phone Monday – Sunday from 08:00 – 20:00 on: **0800 408 1100**
*   Outside of this time, customers can leave a message for the team, and someone will respond as soon as possible.For customers outside of the UK, or those who would prefer to contact us via email, customers can email us via our contact us page on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance)
*   We have a minicom system for customers who are D/deaf or hard of hearing which is open Monday – Sunday, 06:00-20:00 on: **0345 700 7706**
*   We also have a British Sign Language (BSL) Video Relay Service in partnership with Convo, who can contact our Accessibility team via phone Monday – Sunday, 08:00-20:00
*   Customers can find out more by visiting our website or by speaking to a member of the Accessibility team by phone or email

**SUPPORTING OUR CUSTOMERS BEFORE THEY TRAVEL**

**Dedicated pre-travel customer care team**

At British Airways, we have our own dedicated Accessibility team to provide specialist support for customers who require additional assistance, designed to ensure every journey they take with us is as straightforward and stress-free as possible.

Our hand-picked team of Customer Service professionals receive specialist training, to enable them to answer any questions customers have when they get in touch with us. Our team help customers understand what to expect during their journey.

Customers can contact our team prior to making a booking, or once a booking has been made, for support and advice. Once a booking has been made, customers can also log in to Manage My Booking to let us know the type of assistance needed up to 48 hours before the flight is due to depart. We offer assistance with mobility,for those who are D/deaf and hard of hearing, blind and with low vision and non-visible disabilities.

The team can also help customers make new flight, hotel and car hire bookings, arrange bespoke assistance, pre-book seating, inform airport staff and Cabin Crew about specific requirements, and provide information and support to empower customers to have the confidence to fly.

**SUPPORTING CUSTOMERS WITH ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS**

**We have invested in a range of services to support customers who require additional assistance, designed to help ensure that they travel safely, with dignity and in comfort.**

**VISUAL GUIDE TO FLYING**

British Airways offers customers with autism a Visual Guide to Flying, to help them prepare for their flight. We were the first UK airline to be awarded the renowned Autism Friendly Award by the National Autistic Society and became the first airline to produce a Visual Guide to Flying, in partnership with Learning Rose. The guide, which can be found on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance), is endorsed by the National Autistic Society and explains the sights, sounds, smells and experiences customers may encounter during their journey with us.

**CONVO**

British Airways has partnered with Convo to use British Sign Language (BSL) in our contact centres. Customers that use BSL can contact us using a Video Relay Service provided by Convo, a free service that will connect customers to a qualified online BSL interpreter. The interpreter will relay the conversation between the customer and a member of British Airways’ Accessibility team.

**HEARLO**

British Airways has partnered with Hearlo, a smartphone app that helps customers with speech or hearing disabilities, or those facing communication barriers, travel more independently.

The Hearlo app was designed to make interactions smooth and dignified, both on the ground and in the air. It offers features like text-to-speech, instant translation to more than ten languages, and use offline – ideal for international travel.

From check-in to boarding and in-flight services, customers can type messages or select a Hearlo Card - simple pictograms for each stage of the journey. When a card is chosen, the app speaks a full sentence aloud, bridging communication gaps quickly and clearly to help British Airways customers communicate easily with airport colleagues and cabin crew.

Hearlo is available on the [Apple](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hearlo/id1386834397)and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=appinventor.ai_mateo_nicolas_salvatto.Sordos)app store for free.

**SUPPORTING OUR CUSTOMERS AT THE AIRPORT AND ONBOARD**

A range of services are available to our customers at the airport, and we work closely with our airport partners to make all necessary arrangements.

**Depending on our customers’ individual needs and circumstances, we can arrange:**

*   Assistance or an escort to and from the aircraft
*   Help with stairs, where necessary
*   Transport for wheelchairs and mobility aids with the support of Wilson James, our accessibility service provider at Heathrow

**When on the aircraft, our Cabin Crew can help:**

*   Familiarise customers with their seat and the surrounding area
*   Store and retrieve hand baggage
*   Support customers to move between their seat and the bathroom. All of our aircraft are equipped with an onboard wheelchair
*   Open any packaging of onboard meals, identify meals and the layout of the meal tray
*   Customers can contact our Accessibility team in advance to let us know their requirements or can alert a crew member when onboard

**HIDDEN DISABILITIES SUNFLOWER**

We were the first UK airline to officially recognise the sunflower lanyard, partnering with Hidden Disabilities Sunflower. Customers can choose to wear a sunflower lanyard as an indication that they may require additional support, assistance or simply a little more time when travelling.

Our colleagues are trained to understand what a non-visible disability is, and how to approach and support customers wearing a sunflower lanyard.

**SIGNCODE UK**

We have recently partnered with Signcode UK to further improve our accessibility offering for Deaf and hard-of-hearing customers, with new signed video content containing a variety of helpful travel information being made available to customers both pre-travel and whilst on board.

Signcode UK is an organisation dedicated to ensuring equal access to information, products and services for the Deaf and hard-of-hearing community and specialises in translating key information into signed videos. We have collaborated with the organisation to produce signed videos which can be accessed either via a link or unique QR code, allowing customers to receive personalised video messages in sign language.

The first video, which is available for viewing pre-travel on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance/assistance-available#signcode), offers a comprehensive overview of British Airways' service proposition throughout the entire journey, including booking process, the airport experience, onboard services and the in-flight entertainment offering. It also includes a BSL introduction from Fredrick Da Costa, British Airways’ first Deaf Customer Experience Agent who uses BSL as part of his role.

A second video focuses on onboard safety features and procedures. This video is accessible on ba.com and via a QR code that British Airways Mainline cabin crew will have on their mobile devices on board, giving customers the option to choose between receiving a signed video safety briefing on their personal device, or receiving a personalised briefing delivered by one of our crew face-to-face, which is already offered to Deaf or hard of hearing customers.

**AIRPORT ASSISTANCE AT LONDON HEATHROW**

British Airways has dedicated check-in areas at London Heathrow for customers requiring additional assistance and for families with young children.

**AIRPORT ASSISTANCE IN INDIA**

In a bid to improve accessibility for Indian customers travelling from our five Indian hubs to London, British Airways now offers a new in-person service available in local languages. This free “meet and assist service” offers in-person guidance for those with assistance requirements, helping customers to check-in, navigate the airport, find their seat and help with any questions.

**TRAINING AND SUPPORTING OUR COLLEAGUES**

**Colleague training, internal tools and resources**

In 2018 we launched our ‘Beyond Accessibility’ campaign, our largest global accessibility training programme for British Airways’ colleagues. This programme empowers customer facing colleagues to improve support for customers requiring additional assistance. It includes a library of digital learning, providing information about visible and non-visible disabilities and practical advice on how to support customers at each stage of their journey.

We are always updating our training and working with different organisations and charities across the accessibility space to ensure our colleagues are providing the best support to customers. For example, colleagues recently underwent training with Colostomy UK. We also have a partnership with Alzheimer’s UK to help raise awareness and train our colleagues to support any customers with dementia when flying.

In addition, we regularly engage with our colleagues through our colleague network group ‘Being Accessible’ to further support our customers and colleagues with visible and non-visible disabilities, trial new products and services and offer feedback on new products and initiatives.

**WORKING WITH ORGANISATIONS AND GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE FURTHER SUPPORT**

British Airways is part of the Accessibility Working Group chaired by IATA (International Air Transport Association), working to support the industry in delivering the best possible service for customers who have additional requirements, sharing best practice across airlines and engaging with the community.

We have played an active role in The Mobility Aids Action Group, helping IATA develop new guidelines around handling mobility devices.

We have a longstanding relationship with the Business Disability Forum which offers best practice advice and guidance and ensures we remain up to date with changing developments. In addition, we are part of the government’s Disability Confident scheme.

We also work closely with our airport operators, such as London Heathrow and London Gatwick, as well as suppliers across the globe, to provide extra assistance for customers when travelling through the airport.

British Airways works with a variety of organisations and charities to support and enhance our accessibility offering.

We were delighted to be ranked as the best-performing UK airline for website accessibility in a recent report published by the CAA for our user-friendly Digital Accessibility proposition and will continue to work hard to review and improve our offering.

Download the full Accessibility fact sheet [here](https://www.pressarea.com/factsheets/downloadext_assets/86/216/BritishAirwaysAccessibilityFactsheetJune2023.pdf)

_We are working hard to improve our accessibility offering for our customers and are continually introducing new initiatives and partnerships to help us on our journey. This document will be updated regularly to reflect all the changes we are making._

# Accessibility at British Airways

 Customer Experience 

![Image 8: British Airways-British Airways Customer Experience Representative-1280x853-ref180261](https://mediacentre.britishairways.com/contents/archives/216/86/images/thumb1280x1683_width/british_airways-british_airways_customer_experience_representative-1280x853-ref180261_8a7c2_thumb.jpg)

**OUR PROMISE**

For millions of people living with a disability, travel can be difficult – and flying can sometimes feel out of reach. More than one million customers who require additional assistance fly with British Airways each year, and we believe our unique British Airways service should be accessible to everyone.

We’re continually improving our service and our ambition is to become the airline of choice for customers with visible and non-visible disabilities. We are committed to doing everything we can to support customers that require additional assistance and provide a seamless travel experience.

**CONTACTING BRITISH AIRWAYS ’ ACCESSIBILITY TEAM**

*   Our accessibility team can be contacted in the UK via phone Monday – Sunday from 08:00 – 20:00 on: **0800 408 1100**
*   Outside of this time, customers can leave a message for the team, and someone will respond as soon as possible.For customers outside of the UK, or those who would prefer to contact us via email, customers can email us via our contact us page on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance)
*   We have a minicom system for customers who are D/deaf or hard of hearing which is open Monday – Sunday, 06:00-20:00 on: **0345 700 7706**
*   We also have a British Sign Language (BSL) Video Relay Service in partnership with Convo, who can contact our Accessibility team via phone Monday – Sunday, 08:00-20:00
*   Customers can find out more by visiting our website or by speaking to a member of the Accessibility team by phone or email

**SUPPORTING OUR CUSTOMERS BEFORE THEY TRAVEL**

**Dedicated pre-travel customer care team**

At British Airways, we have our own dedicated Accessibility team to provide specialist support for customers who require additional assistance, designed to ensure every journey they take with us is as straightforward and stress-free as possible.

Our hand-picked team of Customer Service professionals receive specialist training, to enable them to answer any questions customers have when they get in touch with us. Our team help customers understand what to expect during their journey.

Customers can contact our team prior to making a booking, or once a booking has been made, for support and advice. Once a booking has been made, customers can also log in to Manage My Booking to let us know the type of assistance needed up to 48 hours before the flight is due to depart. We offer assistance with mobility,for those who are D/deaf and hard of hearing, blind and with low vision and non-visible disabilities.

The team can also help customers make new flight, hotel and car hire bookings, arrange bespoke assistance, pre-book seating, inform airport staff and Cabin Crew about specific requirements, and provide information and support to empower customers to have the confidence to fly.

**SUPPORTING CUSTOMERS WITH ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS**

**We have invested in a range of services to support customers who require additional assistance, designed to help ensure that they travel safely, with dignity and in comfort.**

**VISUAL GUIDE TO FLYING**

British Airways offers customers with autism a Visual Guide to Flying, to help them prepare for their flight. We were the first UK airline to be awarded the renowned Autism Friendly Award by the National Autistic Society and became the first airline to produce a Visual Guide to Flying, in partnership with Learning Rose. The guide, which can be found on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance), is endorsed by the National Autistic Society and explains the sights, sounds, smells and experiences customers may encounter during their journey with us.

**CONVO**

British Airways has partnered with Convo to use British Sign Language (BSL) in our contact centres. Customers that use BSL can contact us using a Video Relay Service provided by Convo, a free service that will connect customers to a qualified online BSL interpreter. The interpreter will relay the conversation between the customer and a member of British Airways’ Accessibility team.

**HEARLO**

British Airways has partnered with Hearlo, a smartphone app that helps customers with speech or hearing disabilities, or those facing communication barriers, travel more independently.

The Hearlo app was designed to make interactions smooth and dignified, both on the ground and in the air. It offers features like text-to-speech, instant translation to more than ten languages, and use offline – ideal for international travel.

From check-in to boarding and in-flight services, customers can type messages or select a Hearlo Card - simple pictograms for each stage of the journey. When a card is chosen, the app speaks a full sentence aloud, bridging communication gaps quickly and clearly to help British Airways customers communicate easily with airport colleagues and cabin crew.

Hearlo is available on the [Apple](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hearlo/id1386834397)and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=appinventor.ai_mateo_nicolas_salvatto.Sordos)app store for free.

**SUPPORTING OUR CUSTOMERS AT THE AIRPORT AND ONBOARD**

A range of services are available to our customers at the airport, and we work closely with our airport partners to make all necessary arrangements.

**Depending on our customers’ individual needs and circumstances, we can arrange:**

*   Assistance or an escort to and from the aircraft
*   Help with stairs, where necessary
*   Transport for wheelchairs and mobility aids with the support of Wilson James, our accessibility service provider at Heathrow

**When on the aircraft, our Cabin Crew can help:**

*   Familiarise customers with their seat and the surrounding area
*   Store and retrieve hand baggage
*   Support customers to move between their seat and the bathroom. All of our aircraft are equipped with an onboard wheelchair
*   Open any packaging of onboard meals, identify meals and the layout of the meal tray
*   Customers can contact our Accessibility team in advance to let us know their requirements or can alert a crew member when onboard

**HIDDEN DISABILITIES SUNFLOWER**

We were the first UK airline to officially recognise the sunflower lanyard, partnering with Hidden Disabilities Sunflower. Customers can choose to wear a sunflower lanyard as an indication that they may require additional support, assistance or simply a little more time when travelling.

Our colleagues are trained to understand what a non-visible disability is, and how to approach and support customers wearing a sunflower lanyard.

**SIGNCODE UK**

We have recently partnered with Signcode UK to further improve our accessibility offering for Deaf and hard-of-hearing customers, with new signed video content containing a variety of helpful travel information being made available to customers both pre-travel and whilst on board.

Signcode UK is an organisation dedicated to ensuring equal access to information, products and services for the Deaf and hard-of-hearing community and specialises in translating key information into signed videos. We have collaborated with the organisation to produce signed videos which can be accessed either via a link or unique QR code, allowing customers to receive personalised video messages in sign language.

The first video, which is available for viewing pre-travel on [ba.com](https://www.britishairways.com/en-gb/information/disability-assistance/assistance-available#signcode), offers a comprehensive overview of British Airways' service proposition throughout the entire journey, including booking process, the airport experience, onboard services and the in-flight entertainment offering. It also includes a BSL introduction from Fredrick Da Costa, British Airways’ first Deaf Customer Experience Agent who uses BSL as part of his role.

A second video focuses on onboard safety features and procedures. This video is accessible on ba.com and via a QR code that British Airways Mainline cabin crew will have on their mobile devices on board, giving customers the option to choose between receiving a signed video safety briefing on their personal device, or receiving a personalised briefing delivered by one of our crew face-to-face, which is already offered to Deaf or hard of hearing customers.

**AIRPORT ASSISTANCE AT LONDON HEATHROW**

British Airways has dedicated check-in areas at London Heathrow for customers requiring additional assistance and for families with young children.

**AIRPORT ASSISTANCE IN INDIA**

In a bid to improve accessibility for Indian customers travelling from our five Indian hubs to London, British Airways now offers a new in-person service available in local languages. This free “meet and assist service” offers in-person guidance for those with assistance requirements, helping customers to check-in, navigate the airport, find their seat and help with any questions.

**TRAINING AND SUPPORTING OUR COLLEAGUES**

**Colleague training, internal tools and resources**

In 2018 we launched our ‘Beyond Accessibility’ campaign, our largest global accessibility training programme for British Airways’ colleagues. This programme empowers customer facing colleagues to improve support for customers requiring additional assistance. It includes a library of digital learning, providing information about visible and non-visible disabilities and practical advice on how to support customers at each stage of their journey.

We are always updating our training and working with different organisations and charities across the accessibility space to ensure our colleagues are providing the best support to customers. For example, colleagues recently underwent training with Colostomy UK. We also have a partnership with Alzheimer’s UK to help raise awareness and train our colleagues to support any customers with dementia when flying.

In addition, we regularly engage with our colleagues through our colleague network group ‘Being Accessible’ to further support our customers and colleagues with visible and non-visible disabilities, trial new products and services and offer feedback on new products and initiatives.

**WORKING WITH ORGANISATIONS AND GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE FURTHER SUPPORT**

British Airways is part of the Accessibility Working Group chaired by IATA (International Air Transport Association), working to support the industry in delivering the best possible service for customers who have additional requirements, sharing best practice across airlines and engaging with the community.

We have played an active role in The Mobility Aids Action Group, helping IATA develop new guidelines around handling mobility devices.

We have a longstanding relationship with the Business Disability Forum which offers best practice advice and guidance and ensures we remain up to date with changing developments. In addition, we are part of the government’s Disability Confident scheme.

We also work closely with our airport operators, such as London Heathrow and London Gatwick, as well as suppliers across the globe, to provide extra assistance for customers when travelling through the airport.

British Airways works with a variety of organisations and charities to support and enhance our accessibility offering.

We were delighted to be ranked as the best-performing UK airline for website accessibility in a recent report published by the CAA for our user-friendly Digital Accessibility proposition and will continue to work hard to review and improve our offering.

Download the full Accessibility fact sheet [here](https://www.pressarea.com/factsheets/downloadext_assets/86/216/BritishAirwaysAccessibilityFactsheetJune2023.pdf)

_We are working hard to improve our accessibility offering for our customers and are continually introducing new initiatives and partnerships to help us on our journey. This document will be updated regularly to reflect all the changes we are making._

10 th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Chair, Select Committee on Transport House of Commons London SW1A 0AA By email: iain.stewart.mp@parliament.uk Dear Mr Stewart 

Air traffic control disruption hearing 

Thank you for offering the opportunity to provide written evidence to support your committee’s session on air traffic control (ATC) disruption. British Airways plays a unique role in connecting Britain with the world. We fly 260 aircraft to nearly 200 destinations in more than 70 countries and connect 10 cities in the regions of the UK with the world via our hub in London. No other UK airline operates long and short haul flights nor offers so much choice to its customers whether for connections or choice of cabin and on-board facilities. As such our operations and our customers’ experiences were uniquely affected by the failure of NATS' IT systems on 28 August this year. We welcome the Committee’s interest in NATS’ performance and the independent review recently announced by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) of the incident and of NATS’ performance more widely. Cause of the Incident We understand that the cause of the outage was a failure of one of NATS’ flight planning systems to cope with a particular combination of duplicate waypoint data being fed into the system as part of one valid flight plan, following its processing by Eurocontrol, that caused both the primary system to fail and its backup to enter a fail-safe mode. We understand this outcome was partly the result of the vital need in such a safety critical system for caution. We have discussed the situation at length with NATS and we have no reason to dispute the outcome of their Major Incident Preliminary View published on 4 September which summarises the initial findings of the event. We support the CAA’s review, which will subject the NATS report to further analysis, and establish the facts over what occurred. We are reassured to hear that the software that caused this incident has been updated to prevent reoccurrence of that specific issue. /2 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 2 of 6 It is clear, however, that there are some fundamental aspects of the failure that resulted in a worse impact than otherwise might have been the case. For example, the fact that only four hours of stored flight data is available in the event of such an outage is disappointing. We note that the resources and resilience of NATS’ business and its ability to recover from such major incidents forms part of the scope of the independent review and we look forward to the outcome and any recommendations on contingency plans. Impacts of the outage Given that every British Airways service arrives at or departs from the UK, we rely on NATS’ service for the navigation of all our flights and their outage therefore caused significant disruption to our customers. Although NATS’ service resumed on the day, the outage had a considerable knock on effect. Over the three-day period of 28-30 August we cancelled 396 flights as a direct result of the failure, meaning that thousands of customers were disrupted. Cancellations were required for subsequent days because of the impacts on British Airways’ resources and planned schedule. When one flight is cancelled, aircraft and crew are often not in their planned position and often unable to operate the anticipated return service. By way of example, a delay to a long haul service for a reason such as bad weather can be accommodated. But if the flight arrives at its destination much later than planned, the crew must still adhere to the minimum regulatory requirements for rest as set by the CAA for safety reasons prior to operating the next flight on their roster, which can cause knock-on disruption to our operation. In this case, 32 aircraft were out of position due to flight and cabin crew reaching their maximum legal flight duty period over the days following the outage. Whilst we anticipate and prepare for scenarios like this during normal operations with standby crew always available, when there is very extensive disruption to the schedule, as was the case in this instance, despite our best efforts, it is not possible to have contingency measures for every flight. Further disruption is often caused by the residual impact of retrieving customers’ bags. Customers will check their hold baggage into the system prior to departure having arrived at the airport well in advance. If their flight is cancelled, the recovery and return of these bags to customers requires considerable resource from a number of stakeholders and puts additional strain on the operation. The fact that the incident occurred on the August Bank Holiday Monday was particularly unfortunate. Not only was it an extremely busy day in itself with many families returning from summer holidays, but reaccommodating disrupted customers on subsequent days, on either our own flights or other airline’s services was much harder because of the season and levels of demand that week. Actions to support our customers 

British Airways’ actions to mitigate the impact of external disruptions and any customers whose flights were affected by the incident were extensive. British Airways was informed of the incident at around 11:30 local time. As soon as the extent of the problem was understood, we immediately set up a Gold Command crisis management team. This well-established procedure is the highest level of crisis management and allows us to make focused, immediate decisions to recover as quickly as possible. /3 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 3 of 6 Initially, we attempted to hold flights and operate with delays rather than cancel them, which is always a preference, but the extent of the impact meant that more than 250 flights had to be cancelled on 28 August. When a British Airways flight is cancelled, our teams automatically send a notification to the customer contact details noted within the booking. It was no different in this case and all those affected were offered a range of options, including rebooking onto alternative services, on other carriers as well as British Airways services, or offered the option of a full refund. Their rights in terms of the duty of care we owe passengers are also explained to them. To help get customers to where they needed to be as quickly as possible and allow us to reaccommodate those disrupted, we also invoked our middle-seat policy in our Club Europe business class cabin (as part of our premium product offer these seats are not usually sold). Making this capacity available added more than 8,000 seats across our short-haul (European) network in the three days following the outage. We also activated our Customer Support Scheme, where volunteers from across the business move from their usual jobs into customer support roles in airport terminals or to support colleagues handling telephone calls and social media enquiries so as to assist our customers as much as possible. Throughout this period our teams liaised with the Department for Transport officials to keep them updated. We also dealt with several cases raised by the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office of vulnerable customers who would otherwise be stranded abroad, to ensure they were in touch with families or had suitable accommodation or could be reaccommodated. Costs incurred by airlines and independent review of NATS 

Despite the incident being clearly the result of a failure by NATS, airlines have legal and financial responsibility for providing care for customers who are disrupted. This includes providing food and drink (or vouchers to buy food and drink), phone calls and accommodation (plus transport to and from the accommodation) and the cost of buying tickets on other airlines where necessary – and we are obliged to cover these costs this until the passenger reaches their destination. In some circumstances, we have to ask customers to book their own accommodation and claim it back (guidance on what can be claimed is available via a dedicated help section of our website (Ba.com/helpme) and within disruption booklets at our airports). Since in this case the difficulty of reaccommodating passengers was increased, the associated costs of looking after passengers for a longer period was naturally higher. The Committee will be aware that customers are also entitled to additional compensation for cancellations or delays under EU261/2004 (applicable in the UK under the EU Withdrawal Act) but will also understand that compensation is not due if the delay or cancellation is due to extraordinary circumstances. Since the failure of NATS is covered by such a definition, compensation is not due in this case. The duty of care costs British Airways incurred as a result of this outage are substantial and it is not reasonable for airlines to bear the financial burden. /4 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 4 of 6 There is, however, no established mechanism for NATS to repay airlines in such circumstances. The Transport Act indemnifies NATS for the impacts of failures such as those resulting from this outage and while the economic regulatory regime includes the ability to penalise NATS for failing to keep overall delays within certain limits, the penalties are limited and there is no provision to penalise NATS for causing flights to be cancelled. The CAA’s independent review is the appropriate vehicle to consider whether NATS’ incentives should be amended to account for future such incidents. It has the appropriate scope since not only will it look at the technical causes of the failure and remediation taken by NATS, but also consider broader matters relating to NATS’ resilience and performance as a regulated business, the impact on consumers, and the current UK framework for allocating costs to airlines for events outside their control. Given the extent of the review, I wrote recently to the Secretary of State for Transport to reinforce our belief that it is important that at least one member of the panel should be able to offer expertise in consumer protection and the economics of regulated businesses. British Airways’ colleagues work hard to give our customers the best experience we can and it is our duty to look after them when things go wrong. But it cannot be right that we must be financially liable through EU(UK)261 for problems caused by others whether, in this case an air navigation services provider (ANSP), or by airports or ground handlers. It seems to us that the priority for the review team should be to consider whether expanding the scope of EU(UK)261 to make NATS and other parties responsible for duty of care costs should they be responsible for cancellations or delays, would provide a better balance of responsibilities and incentivise better performance across the aviation system. Relationship with NATS 

In the light of media coverage following the incident and given the comments made by other airlines at the hearing on Wednesday 18 October, I hope it will assist the Committee if I explain our approach to the relationship with NATS. NATS is an essential provider of air navigation services in the UK and one of the most important of all suppliers to British Airways. It is therefore in our highest interest to see that NATS performs well and provides efficient, uninterrupted service, to maintain our operations to the benefit of our own customers. British Airways paid NATS tens of millions of pounds in charges for navigation services in 2022 so we have an obvious interest in receiving a good service in return. When it comes to costs, we have participated actively in the CAA’s recent price control review of NATS’ charges for en route and certain traffic services. As NATS is the monopoly provider for those services, we have contributed in detail to ensure the most efficient outcome for us and our customers. At the same time, we believe that NERL must be incentivised to provide a safe, resilient and high-quality service. On 26 October, the CAA issued its Final Decision on NATS’s price control, setting out a price increase for the 2023-2027 period. We are reviewing the CAA’s decision and are considering our next steps. Although primarily our relationship with NATS is as a customer, we also see the organisation as a vital part of the UK’s aviation infrastructure and it is in our interests to be involved more closely. /5 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 5 of 6 You will be aware that after HM Government with 48.9%, the Airline Group is the second largest shareholder with 41.9% of NATS. The Airline Group is a consortium made up of five airlines or airline groups (British Airways, easyJet, Deutsche Lufthansa, TUI and Virgin Atlantic) and two institutional investors (Universities Superannuation Scheme (USS) and the Pension Protection Fund). British Airways’ share of the Airline Group means it owns just over 7% of the whole of NATS. We hold this interest not for the primary purpose of receiving a commercial return on our investment, or to have operational say over NATS, but so as to have oversight and involvement with an organisation we see as an important strategic partner. As key players in the UK aviation industry we have similar interests, from ensuring effective day to day operations to delivering important improvements such as to airspace modernisation that will help us all meet our net zero carbon emissions targets. The Committee should note that NATS last paid its shareholders a dividend in 2019. In that year it paid a total of £57m, and £58m in 2018. Given British Airways’ small shareholding, our costs as a customer are many times the benefit we receive in dividends as a shareholder. Although the Airline Group appoints non-executive directors, operational management of NATS is the clear responsibility of its executive team. We note that representatives of other airlines (including easyJet which holds a stake in NATS) suggested at the hearing that airlines should come together to demand the return of costs incurred through NATS’ IT failure. We believe that these discussions between shareholders should happen through the normal governance process and board activity. Furthermore, we draw attention to the risk of unintended consequences that could result from any changes to NATS’ economic regulation framework without careful assessment, including increased costs for airlines and therefore consumers. We consider that the question of the duty of care costs incurred by airlines in such situations could be better addressed by streamlining the EU(UK)261 framework. Indeed, we hope that the CAA’s independent review will offer an opportunity to improve the framework for allocating costs to airlines for events outside their control and we look forward to the outcomes on this topic as on the rest of its scope. We look forward to the outcomes of the CAA independent review which will also inform this discussion. NATS performance 

We note that the independent review will also consider NATS’ performance relative to its peers. Although this particular incident of service failure had very poor consequences for airlines and their customers it is not typical and NATS does not generally perform badly. Much worse are the restrictions on airspace use due to regular periods of industrial action in France as well as ad hoc but frequent strikes and low resources in other European ANSPs. /6 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 6 of 6 Analysis of Eurocontrol data shows that at Gatwick Airport in 2022 and the first quarter of 2023 NATS was responsible for 9.8% of all arrival delay minutes incurred by British Airways services that are attributed to air traffic control. The other 90% of delays were due to the impacts of restrictions imposed by other ANSPs through the airspace of which flights to Gatwick had to pass. The same figure for Heathrow Airport is 3.6%. Any delays caused by ATC restrictions are unwelcome and it is particularly disappointing that Gatwick has had to impose capacity restrictions due to lack of resources in the control tower for which services are provided by NATS. However, we recognise this is a temporary problem and NATS is working towards increasing the number of controllers qualified to operate in that location. I trust this information is helpful to the committee. Yours sincerely

10 th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Chair, Select Committee on Transport House of Commons London SW1A 0AA By email: iain.stewart.mp@parliament.uk Dear Mr Stewart 

Air traffic control disruption hearing 

Thank you for offering the opportunity to provide written evidence to support your committee’s session on air traffic control (ATC) disruption. British Airways plays a unique role in connecting Britain with the world. We fly 260 aircraft to nearly 200 destinations in more than 70 countries and connect 10 cities in the regions of the UK with the world via our hub in London. No other UK airline operates long and short haul flights nor offers so much choice to its customers whether for connections or choice of cabin and on-board facilities. As such our operations and our customers’ experiences were uniquely affected by the failure of NATS' IT systems on 28 August this year. We welcome the Committee’s interest in NATS’ performance and the independent review recently announced by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) of the incident and of NATS’ performance more widely. Cause of the Incident We understand that the cause of the outage was a failure of one of NATS’ flight planning systems to cope with a particular combination of duplicate waypoint data being fed into the system as part of one valid flight plan, following its processing by Eurocontrol, that caused both the primary system to fail and its backup to enter a fail-safe mode. We understand this outcome was partly the result of the vital need in such a safety critical system for caution. We have discussed the situation at length with NATS and we have no reason to dispute the outcome of their Major Incident Preliminary View published on 4 September which summarises the initial findings of the event. We support the CAA’s review, which will subject the NATS report to further analysis, and establish the facts over what occurred. We are reassured to hear that the software that caused this incident has been updated to prevent reoccurrence of that specific issue. /2 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 2 of 6 It is clear, however, that there are some fundamental aspects of the failure that resulted in a worse impact than otherwise might have been the case. For example, the fact that only four hours of stored flight data is available in the event of such an outage is disappointing. We note that the resources and resilience of NATS’ business and its ability to recover from such major incidents forms part of the scope of the independent review and we look forward to the outcome and any recommendations on contingency plans. Impacts of the outage Given that every British Airways service arrives at or departs from the UK, we rely on NATS’ service for the navigation of all our flights and their outage therefore caused significant disruption to our customers. Although NATS’ service resumed on the day, the outage had a considerable knock on effect. Over the three-day period of 28-30 August we cancelled 396 flights as a direct result of the failure, meaning that thousands of customers were disrupted. Cancellations were required for subsequent days because of the impacts on British Airways’ resources and planned schedule. When one flight is cancelled, aircraft and crew are often not in their planned position and often unable to operate the anticipated return service. By way of example, a delay to a long haul service for a reason such as bad weather can be accommodated. But if the flight arrives at its destination much later than planned, the crew must still adhere to the minimum regulatory requirements for rest as set by the CAA for safety reasons prior to operating the next flight on their roster, which can cause knock-on disruption to our operation. In this case, 32 aircraft were out of position due to flight and cabin crew reaching their maximum legal flight duty period over the days following the outage. Whilst we anticipate and prepare for scenarios like this during normal operations with standby crew always available, when there is very extensive disruption to the schedule, as was the case in this instance, despite our best efforts, it is not possible to have contingency measures for every flight. Further disruption is often caused by the residual impact of retrieving customers’ bags. Customers will check their hold baggage into the system prior to departure having arrived at the airport well in advance. If their flight is cancelled, the recovery and return of these bags to customers requires considerable resource from a number of stakeholders and puts additional strain on the operation. The fact that the incident occurred on the August Bank Holiday Monday was particularly unfortunate. Not only was it an extremely busy day in itself with many families returning from summer holidays, but reaccommodating disrupted customers on subsequent days, on either our own flights or other airline’s services was much harder because of the season and levels of demand that week. Actions to support our customers 

British Airways’ actions to mitigate the impact of external disruptions and any customers whose flights were affected by the incident were extensive. British Airways was informed of the incident at around 11:30 local time. As soon as the extent of the problem was understood, we immediately set up a Gold Command crisis management team. This well-established procedure is the highest level of crisis management and allows us to make focused, immediate decisions to recover as quickly as possible. /3 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 3 of 6 Initially, we attempted to hold flights and operate with delays rather than cancel them, which is always a preference, but the extent of the impact meant that more than 250 flights had to be cancelled on 28 August. When a British Airways flight is cancelled, our teams automatically send a notification to the customer contact details noted within the booking. It was no different in this case and all those affected were offered a range of options, including rebooking onto alternative services, on other carriers as well as British Airways services, or offered the option of a full refund. Their rights in terms of the duty of care we owe passengers are also explained to them. To help get customers to where they needed to be as quickly as possible and allow us to reaccommodate those disrupted, we also invoked our middle-seat policy in our Club Europe business class cabin (as part of our premium product offer these seats are not usually sold). Making this capacity available added more than 8,000 seats across our short-haul (European) network in the three days following the outage. We also activated our Customer Support Scheme, where volunteers from across the business move from their usual jobs into customer support roles in airport terminals or to support colleagues handling telephone calls and social media enquiries so as to assist our customers as much as possible. Throughout this period our teams liaised with the Department for Transport officials to keep them updated. We also dealt with several cases raised by the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office of vulnerable customers who would otherwise be stranded abroad, to ensure they were in touch with families or had suitable accommodation or could be reaccommodated. Costs incurred by airlines and independent review of NATS 

Despite the incident being clearly the result of a failure by NATS, airlines have legal and financial responsibility for providing care for customers who are disrupted. This includes providing food and drink (or vouchers to buy food and drink), phone calls and accommodation (plus transport to and from the accommodation) and the cost of buying tickets on other airlines where necessary – and we are obliged to cover these costs this until the passenger reaches their destination. In some circumstances, we have to ask customers to book their own accommodation and claim it back (guidance on what can be claimed is available via a dedicated help section of our website (Ba.com/helpme) and within disruption booklets at our airports). Since in this case the difficulty of reaccommodating passengers was increased, the associated costs of looking after passengers for a longer period was naturally higher. The Committee will be aware that customers are also entitled to additional compensation for cancellations or delays under EU261/2004 (applicable in the UK under the EU Withdrawal Act) but will also understand that compensation is not due if the delay or cancellation is due to extraordinary circumstances. Since the failure of NATS is covered by such a definition, compensation is not due in this case. The duty of care costs British Airways incurred as a result of this outage are substantial and it is not reasonable for airlines to bear the financial burden. /4 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 4 of 6 There is, however, no established mechanism for NATS to repay airlines in such circumstances. The Transport Act indemnifies NATS for the impacts of failures such as those resulting from this outage and while the economic regulatory regime includes the ability to penalise NATS for failing to keep overall delays within certain limits, the penalties are limited and there is no provision to penalise NATS for causing flights to be cancelled. The CAA’s independent review is the appropriate vehicle to consider whether NATS’ incentives should be amended to account for future such incidents. It has the appropriate scope since not only will it look at the technical causes of the failure and remediation taken by NATS, but also consider broader matters relating to NATS’ resilience and performance as a regulated business, the impact on consumers, and the current UK framework for allocating costs to airlines for events outside their control. Given the extent of the review, I wrote recently to the Secretary of State for Transport to reinforce our belief that it is important that at least one member of the panel should be able to offer expertise in consumer protection and the economics of regulated businesses. British Airways’ colleagues work hard to give our customers the best experience we can and it is our duty to look after them when things go wrong. But it cannot be right that we must be financially liable through EU(UK)261 for problems caused by others whether, in this case an air navigation services provider (ANSP), or by airports or ground handlers. It seems to us that the priority for the review team should be to consider whether expanding the scope of EU(UK)261 to make NATS and other parties responsible for duty of care costs should they be responsible for cancellations or delays, would provide a better balance of responsibilities and incentivise better performance across the aviation system. Relationship with NATS 

In the light of media coverage following the incident and given the comments made by other airlines at the hearing on Wednesday 18 October, I hope it will assist the Committee if I explain our approach to the relationship with NATS. NATS is an essential provider of air navigation services in the UK and one of the most important of all suppliers to British Airways. It is therefore in our highest interest to see that NATS performs well and provides efficient, uninterrupted service, to maintain our operations to the benefit of our own customers. British Airways paid NATS tens of millions of pounds in charges for navigation services in 2022 so we have an obvious interest in receiving a good service in return. When it comes to costs, we have participated actively in the CAA’s recent price control review of NATS’ charges for en route and certain traffic services. As NATS is the monopoly provider for those services, we have contributed in detail to ensure the most efficient outcome for us and our customers. At the same time, we believe that NERL must be incentivised to provide a safe, resilient and high-quality service. On 26 October, the CAA issued its Final Decision on NATS’s price control, setting out a price increase for the 2023-2027 period. We are reviewing the CAA’s decision and are considering our next steps. Although primarily our relationship with NATS is as a customer, we also see the organisation as a vital part of the UK’s aviation infrastructure and it is in our interests to be involved more closely. /5 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 5 of 6 You will be aware that after HM Government with 48.9%, the Airline Group is the second largest shareholder with 41.9% of NATS. The Airline Group is a consortium made up of five airlines or airline groups (British Airways, easyJet, Deutsche Lufthansa, TUI and Virgin Atlantic) and two institutional investors (Universities Superannuation Scheme (USS) and the Pension Protection Fund). British Airways’ share of the Airline Group means it owns just over 7% of the whole of NATS. We hold this interest not for the primary purpose of receiving a commercial return on our investment, or to have operational say over NATS, but so as to have oversight and involvement with an organisation we see as an important strategic partner. As key players in the UK aviation industry we have similar interests, from ensuring effective day to day operations to delivering important improvements such as to airspace modernisation that will help us all meet our net zero carbon emissions targets. The Committee should note that NATS last paid its shareholders a dividend in 2019. In that year it paid a total of £57m, and £58m in 2018. Given British Airways’ small shareholding, our costs as a customer are many times the benefit we receive in dividends as a shareholder. Although the Airline Group appoints non-executive directors, operational management of NATS is the clear responsibility of its executive team. We note that representatives of other airlines (including easyJet which holds a stake in NATS) suggested at the hearing that airlines should come together to demand the return of costs incurred through NATS’ IT failure. We believe that these discussions between shareholders should happen through the normal governance process and board activity. Furthermore, we draw attention to the risk of unintended consequences that could result from any changes to NATS’ economic regulation framework without careful assessment, including increased costs for airlines and therefore consumers. We consider that the question of the duty of care costs incurred by airlines in such situations could be better addressed by streamlining the EU(UK)261 framework. Indeed, we hope that the CAA’s independent review will offer an opportunity to improve the framework for allocating costs to airlines for events outside their control and we look forward to the outcomes on this topic as on the rest of its scope. We look forward to the outcomes of the CAA independent review which will also inform this discussion. NATS performance 

We note that the independent review will also consider NATS’ performance relative to its peers. Although this particular incident of service failure had very poor consequences for airlines and their customers it is not typical and NATS does not generally perform badly. Much worse are the restrictions on airspace use due to regular periods of industrial action in France as well as ad hoc but frequent strikes and low resources in other European ANSPs. /6 10th November 2023 Iain Stewart MP Page 6 of 6 Analysis of Eurocontrol data shows that at Gatwick Airport in 2022 and the first quarter of 2023 NATS was responsible for 9.8% of all arrival delay minutes incurred by British Airways services that are attributed to air traffic control. The other 90% of delays were due to the impacts of restrictions imposed by other ANSPs through the airspace of which flights to Gatwick had to pass. The same figure for Heathrow Airport is 3.6%. Any delays caused by ATC restrictions are unwelcome and it is particularly disappointing that Gatwick has had to impose capacity restrictions due to lack of resources in the control tower for which services are provided by NATS. However, we recognise this is a temporary problem and NATS is working towards increasing the number of controllers qualified to operate in that location. I trust this information is helpful to the committee. Yours sincerely

# Airline passengers in UK being let down by ‘toothless regulation’

This article is more than 3 years old

Which? calls for stronger legislation, saying no airline has been fined for breaching obligations in 20 years

[Gwyn Topham](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/gwyntopham) Transport correspondent

Fri 30 Jun 2023 01.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Jun 2023 01.36 EDT

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

Airline passengers in the UK are being let down by toothless regulation, with no airline fined in the last 20 years for breaching obligations, the consumer group Which? has found.

It called for urgent legislation to beef up the regulator’s powers, contrasting the lack of action in the UK over [unpaid refunds](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/dec/16/airlines-failure-to-offer-covid-cash-refunds-investigated-by-uk-regulator) or compensation with fines issued in other countries.

The Civil Aviation Authority was given powers in June 2003 to apply to courts to ensure enforcement against airlines for consumer protection. It has only pursued that course of action once, however, against Ryanair in 2018, in a case that ended with the airline agreeing to pay due compensation to passengers but no further sanction.

Authorities in the US this month [fined British Airways $1.1m](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/jun/01/us-fines-british-airways-11m-for-failing-to-refund-covid-cancellations) after 1,200 complaints about delayed refunds during the pandemic, but the carrier has not faced any similar threat in the UK over affected customers.

British law requires airlines to issue refunds for cancellations within seven days, but many passengers waited months during the pandemic.

CAA data from 2020 alone also showed more than 24,000 complaints recorded over compensation under the EU261, due from airlines for cancelled or delayed flights. Italy, Germany and Greece are among the other nations whose regulators have fined airlines in recent years.

Which? said the CAA should be doing more to pursue law-breaking airlines and urgently needed stronger enforcement powers.

The Department for Transport announced this week that it plans to give the CAA the power to fine airlines “when parliamentary time allows”.

Which? urged the government to act without delay and legislate in the next King’s Speech. Its director of policy Rocio Concha said: “The US government fining Britain’s flag carrier when our own authorities are powerless to do the same makes a mockery of aviation regulation in the UK, which has been failing travellers for 20 years.

“Passengers have repeatedly endured unfair and in some cases unlawful treatment by some airlines in recent years and meaningful action is long past due.”  
  
 Until it gives the regulator powers to hold airlines to account, “UK travellers’ rights will be worth no more than the paper they are written on”, she said.

The CAA’s head of consumer, Anna Bowles, said: “We have regularly asked for stronger consumer enforcement powers, including the ability to impose fines on airlines.”

A BA spokesperson said: “Where a customer’s flight is cancelled, we always offer options including a full refund, rerouting or rebooking on to another service, including with other airlines. We always meet our legal obligations.”

Ryanair said any customers entitled to compensationas a result of staff strikes in 2018 “who applied directly to Ryanair for compensation have received compensation directly from Ryanair in line with EU261”.

# Airline passengers in UK being let down by ‘toothless regulation’

This article is more than 3 years old

Which? calls for stronger legislation, saying no airline has been fined for breaching obligations in 20 years

[Gwyn Topham](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/gwyntopham) Transport correspondent

Fri 30 Jun 2023 01.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Jun 2023 01.36 EDT

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

Airline passengers in the UK are being let down by toothless regulation, with no airline fined in the last 20 years for breaching obligations, the consumer group Which? has found.

It called for urgent legislation to beef up the regulator’s powers, contrasting the lack of action in the UK over [unpaid refunds](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/dec/16/airlines-failure-to-offer-covid-cash-refunds-investigated-by-uk-regulator) or compensation with fines issued in other countries.

The Civil Aviation Authority was given powers in June 2003 to apply to courts to ensure enforcement against airlines for consumer protection. It has only pursued that course of action once, however, against Ryanair in 2018, in a case that ended with the airline agreeing to pay due compensation to passengers but no further sanction.

Authorities in the US this month [fined British Airways $1.1m](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/jun/01/us-fines-british-airways-11m-for-failing-to-refund-covid-cancellations) after 1,200 complaints about delayed refunds during the pandemic, but the carrier has not faced any similar threat in the UK over affected customers.

British law requires airlines to issue refunds for cancellations within seven days, but many passengers waited months during the pandemic.

CAA data from 2020 alone also showed more than 24,000 complaints recorded over compensation under the EU261, due from airlines for cancelled or delayed flights. Italy, Germany and Greece are among the other nations whose regulators have fined airlines in recent years.

Which? said the CAA should be doing more to pursue law-breaking airlines and urgently needed stronger enforcement powers.

The Department for Transport announced this week that it plans to give the CAA the power to fine airlines “when parliamentary time allows”.

Which? urged the government to act without delay and legislate in the next King’s Speech. Its director of policy Rocio Concha said: “The US government fining Britain’s flag carrier when our own authorities are powerless to do the same makes a mockery of aviation regulation in the UK, which has been failing travellers for 20 years.

“Passengers have repeatedly endured unfair and in some cases unlawful treatment by some airlines in recent years and meaningful action is long past due.”  
  
 Until it gives the regulator powers to hold airlines to account, “UK travellers’ rights will be worth no more than the paper they are written on”, she said.

The CAA’s head of consumer, Anna Bowles, said: “We have regularly asked for stronger consumer enforcement powers, including the ability to impose fines on airlines.”

A BA spokesperson said: “Where a customer’s flight is cancelled, we always offer options including a full refund, rerouting or rebooking on to another service, including with other airlines. We always meet our legal obligations.”

Ryanair said any customers entitled to compensationas a result of staff strikes in 2018 “who applied directly to Ryanair for compensation have received compensation directly from Ryanair in line with EU261”.
